title: Who will keep the lights on? Gas supply, green gas and a fair transition
label: 4 November 2026 · Managing the future of UK oil and gas
summary: The Committee questioned gas network operators, biomethane industry leaders and trade bodies about UK gas supply, storage, the potential of biomethane, hydrogen’s role, costs of keeping the network running and how to avoid unfairly burdening remaining gas users as demand falls. Witnesses agreed gas will remain important for years, said UK biomethane could grow substantially and boost jobs, and warned that decommissioning or a rapid switch could leave vulnerable people and workers exposed without a clear national plan.

chapters.title: How much UK gas do we have and what does it serve?
chapters.takeaway: Domestic production is useful but limited; imports, storage and the network all play key roles in meeting peak winter demand.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start: how much can the UK rely on domestic gas for electricity, heat and industry?

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: We have North Sea gas and growing biomethane potential, but imports will remain part of the mix.

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: On average UK production covers about 40–45% of demand. Daily peak domestic output is roughly 100 million cubic metres, but winter peak can hit 500 million—so domestic covers about 20% then.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does Government policy favour imports over domestic production?

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: We need imports in winter. Policy should ensure markets attract LNG and interconnector flows; domestic supply helps security but doesn’t remove the need to import.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can increasing domestic production bring prices down?

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: Evidence from Jackdaw suggests not necessarily for price, but more domestic supply improves energy security.

chapters.title: Biomethane: how big could it be and what would it change?
chapters.takeaway: Biomethane can grow a lot, provide stable-priced gas, create local jobs, and displace some imports—if policy and funding are clear.

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: There are 140 biomethane plants now, enough to decarbonise about 1 million homes invisibly.

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Our analysis says the UK has sustainable feedstock to reach about 120 TWh of biomethane by 2050—over ten times today; NESO found a similar 109 TWh for GB.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How realistic is that tenfold increase?

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Realistic: the supply chain exists. If Government set a long-term policy framework, bigger plants and co-products could cut costs.

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Average UK production cost is about £90/MWh today; with scale and valorising co-benefits we estimate roughly a 25% cost reduction could be achievable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about jobs and local benefits?

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: If maximised, biomethane could support about 57,000 jobs nationwide—skilled engineering roles, spread across constituencies and keeping 85p of every £1 in the UK supply chain.

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: Networks can take biomethane where there’s demand; sometimes reinforcement is needed but costs are not huge and are usually paid by producers today.

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Working closely with gas networks is vital—without the networks biomethane would be costlier to deliver.

chapters.title: Storage, system flexibility and energy security
chapters.takeaway: The UK's storage model is flexible daily balancing rather than huge seasonal stores; diversity of supply (LNG, interconnectors, storage) supports security, but policy clarity is needed.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: We have less UK and EU storage than in previous years—what does that mean for security this winter?

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: GB storage operates differently to continental sites: ours fill and empty quickly and provide daily flexibility. They help the market balance every day.

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: UK supply is five sources: domestic production, Norway, interconnectors, LNG and storage/linepack. Together they provide the flexibility needed—if markets and contracts work.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: What about floating storage regasification units (FSRUs) or a strategic reserve?

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: FSRUs can be part of an answer; they provide short-term supply. The Government’s gas system transition consultation should set a security standard and then options—FSRUs, strategic sites, contracts—can be compared.

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: We run annual exercises for outages, cyber or supply shortages to test responses and protect vulnerable customers—preparedness matters.

chapters.title: Emissions, hydrogen and the role of gas to 2050
chapters.takeaway: Gas is expected to remain part of the net‑zero system alongside hydrogen and biomethane; hydrogen will need clear policy support and biomethane has strict carbon requirements.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How green is biomethane compared with LNG or North Sea gas?

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Biomethane avoids emissions that would otherwise be released by rotting waste; UK projects must demonstrate at least a 70% carbon saving to get support, and many do better.

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: Simpler: biomethane is short-cycle carbon—plants regrow—so burning it doesn't add fossil carbon to the atmosphere the way long-cycle fossil gas does.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about nitrogen oxide (NOx) from burning methane?

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: Boiler standards reduce NOx emissions; network operators don't manufacture boilers, so technical detail would come from appliance specialists.

turns.speaker: Catherine Fookes
turns.text: Can hydrogen substitute gas for heating?

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: Hydrogen has a role—NESO’s holistic scenario includes around 100 TWh—particularly for industry and power where electrification is hard. It can be made in the UK, including from surplus wind, but policy and funding certainty are needed.

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: The existing network can carry 100% hydrogen if repurposed, or a blend around 20%, but you can't carry both natural gas and hydrogen in the same pipes without change.

chapters.title: Costs, decommissioning risk and the workforce
chapters.takeaway: Shrinking the gas system without a clear national plan risks high bills for remaining users, unfair cost distribution and disrupted careers; hybrids and biomethane were suggested as pragmatic bridges.

turns.speaker: Torcuil Crichton
turns.text: If fewer people use gas, who pays to maintain the network? Some estimates say £100bn.

turns.speaker: Jenny Phillips
turns.text: Transmission’s recent price control was about £5bn over five years; electricity had much larger recent allowances. Keeping networks safe costs money—about £12.50 on bills was cited for transmission recovery.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: If decommissioning happens the costs should be spread widely—general taxation is fairer than leaving the last users to carry the bill.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: Today an average domestic contribution for the gas network is around £122/year. If customer numbers halve, fixed costs might double; if only a few million remain, fixed charges could become very large for those households.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: I advise against a policy that ends with cutting people off from gas—heating, hot water and cooking depend on it for many households.

turns.speaker: Rhea Wolfson
turns.text: Workers need a real, funded national plan. Skills are transferable but without clear demand the jobs for trained staff don’t materialise and people leave the sector.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: Heat pump roll-out is too slow—about 45,000 installs a year at current rates—far short of what decarbonisation targets imply. Hybrids are being installed only in the hundreds.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: Hybrids (small heat pump + gas boiler) cut carbon by c.80% and are cheaper to install than full heat pumps; they could be a pragmatic stepping stone. I argued for subsidies for hybrids to increase uptake.

turns.speaker: Wera Hobhouse
turns.text: Is policy certainty good enough? Announcements have been inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Mike Foster
turns.text: Industry needs certainty. I recommended scrapping the Clean Heat Market Mechanism (the so-called boiler tax) and supporting hybrids to get more homes moving now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the clearest near-term asks to Government?

turns.speaker: Charles McAllister
turns.text: Publish the future biomethane framework so investors build. The sector responds quickly to clarity and cheap small incentives—140 plants were built when previous support existed.

turns.speaker: Dr Needle
turns.text: Set clear gas-system transition rules so networks and suppliers know what investments are needed and how costs will be recovered.

turns.speaker: Rhea Wolfson
turns.text: A jobs-first plan with training, no forced redundancies and credible replacement jobs is essential before large-scale decommissioning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Please send any further evidence—this will inform our recommendations to Ministers.
